items.prompt: Fetch 500 URLs (each request spends ~200 ms waiting on the network) and return the total number of bytes downloaded.
items.why: Independent, I/O-bound pieces → a thread pool overlaps the waiting. The GIL is released during I/O, so threads work in Python too.

items.prompt: Count the nodes of a binary tree with about 100 nodes.
items.why: The subtrees are independent, but the work per node is tiny: thread start-up and joins would cost more than the whole traversal. Use a plain recursive DFS.

items.prompt: Follow-up: two binary trees have millions of nodes each and you have 16 cores. Decide whether they are identical as fast as possible.
items.why: Comparing (left, left) and (right, right) are independent, large sub-tasks → fork–join down to a cutoff depth, then sequential DFS. In Python use processes, or Go goroutines, for this CPU-bound work.

items.prompt: Merge k sorted log files into one sorted output stream.
items.why: The hard part is the global order → a min-heap over the k heads. Reading files in parallel doesn't produce the merged order.

items.prompt: Design a fixed-capacity queue shared by producer and consumer threads: enqueue blocks while it is full, dequeue blocks while it is empty.
items.why: 'Blocks while full/empty' across threads → a lock plus a condition variable (or a semaphore pair), with the condition re-checked in a while loop.

items.prompt: Implement an iterator over a BST whose next() should almost never wait, because the caller does heavy work between calls.
items.why: Prefetch: a background thread walks the tree in order and fills a bounded blocking queue, while next() just dequeues. The overlap only pays off because the caller is slow between calls.

items.prompt: Return the minimum number of moves for a knight to reach a target square on an empty chessboard.
items.why: Shortest path in an unweighted graph → BFS. Each level depends on the previous one, so parallelism can't replace the algorithm.

items.prompt: Return the k most frequent words in a 2 GB text file.
items.why: The core is 'k most frequent' → count, then a size-k heap. You could count chunks in parallel, but the selection pattern is Top 'K' Elements.
